title: 61 Animal performance in small ruminant grazing systems on semi-arid savanna rangelands
content:
Abstract
Global records show rising mean annual temperatures and intensified variations in mean annual precipitation. At the Texas A&M AgriLife Sonora Research Station, the decadal coefficient of variation in annual Standardized Precipitation Index values increased from 17.8% in the 1970s to 57.3% in the 2010s. Texas Land Trends projects that Texas will face its largest intergenerational land transfer and potential land-use changes within the next decade. With these changes accelerating, our objective is to provide practical science and education in the context of dynamic climate, economic, and land ownership trends that impact the sustainability of ranching operations in semi-arid savannas. This long-term adaptive resource management experiment will compare the inputs needed for a 4 pasture, 2 herd (+ 1 optional) rotational grazing system (Flex) with those needed for a continuous grazing system (Continuous). The null hypothesis is that there will be no difference between the two management strategies, both managed to reach benchmarks designed to maintain an ecosystem state that supports economically sustainable livestock production, wildlife, and other ecosystem services. Animals used were stratified by body weight (BW) into the two grazing systems at a stocking rate appropriate for the most commonly occurring regional drought 12.14 ha/au. The Flex system was stocked with 29 bred dorper ewes and 30 angora wethers: 1 pasture per species. The Continuous system was stocked with 20 bred dorper ewe sheep and 20 angora wethers. Livestock BW, body condition scores (BCS), and inner eyelid FAMACHA scores (internal parasite marker) were obtained monthly. Animal nutritional status and landscape vegetation modeling were integrated with traditional observational data to guide adaptive grazing and landscape management decisions. After completing 12 months of data collection, a paired-T test was used to compare the species per treatment (sheep vs. sheep, goats vs. goats) and sheep vs. goats (Flex + Continuous vs. Flex + Continuous), to determine if there were any significant differences (P < 0.05) between treatments and species for animal production items of interest (Table 1). The following sheep parameters differed (P < 0.05) by grazing system: BCS, FAMACHA, and lamb weaning weight. There were no differences (P > 0.05) in sheep BW between treatments. Goat FAMACHA scores were greater (P < 0.05) in the Continuous system, and goat BW, BCS, and fleece weights remained similar (P > 0.05). There was a significant (P < 0.05) species difference for BW, BCS, and FAMACHA scores between sheep and goats as expected. These results will be used in extension programming efforts to assist land managers and researchers in reaching ecological and agricultural objectives and provide examples of strategies for small ruminant grazing on semi-arid rangelands in the context of current climate, economic, and land-use goals.
